common_name: Red Siam Chinese Evergreen (Deep Red-Edged Aglaonema)

planting.note: Divide offshoots or plant nursery starts in spring in a well-drained, fertile potting mix in bright indirect light to medium shade; Red Siam holds its deepest red edging when given brighter, filtered light than a typical office corner.

directions: Red Siam is one of the more saturated color selections of the common Chinese evergreen, its lance-shaped leaves washed in deep rose-red toward the margins and midrib against a dark-green base, a bolder color break than the silver-and-green patterning of older commutatum cultivars. Like other Chinese evergreens it tolerates irregular watering, average indoor humidity, and lower light than most houseplants, but the red coloration fades toward plain green in deep shade, so a spot with bright, indirect light keeps the color strongest. Let the top inch or two of potting mix dry between waterings, and avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 60°F, which can cause chilling injury to the leaves. Divide congested clumps every few years to refresh the display and produce new starts.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production and cultivars
North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Aglaonema commutatum
ASPCA Animal Poison Control — Aglaonema (toxic to pets)

common_name: Super White Chinese Evergreen (Near-White Variegated Aglaonema)

planting.note: Divide offshoots or plant nursery starts in spring in a well-drained potting mix in bright, indirect light; Super White needs noticeably more light than green Chinese evergreens because its pale leaves carry little chlorophyll.

directions: Super White is among the palest of the commutatum-type Chinese evergreens, its lance-shaped leaves almost entirely creamy white apart from a thin green rim and scattered green flecking along the veins, giving a striking, almost ghostly look on a compact, upright plant. Because so little chlorophyll remains in the leaf tissue, it needs brighter filtered light than typical low-light Aglaonema to keep growing steadily, though direct sun will still scorch the delicate white areas. Water when the top few inches of mix have dried, and protect it from cold drafts and temperatures below 60°F. Its small size and pale color make it a good fit for desks, shelves, and other spots where a striking accent is wanted at close range.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Aglaonema commutatum
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Aglaonema production and cultivars
ASPCA Animal Poison Control — Aglaonema (toxic to pets)

common_name: White Martagon Lily (Album Turk's Cap Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 4-6 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in partial shade; the white-flowered form thrives under the same woodland conditions as the species and should be left undisturbed once established.

directions: Album strips away the dark spotting and pink-purple wash of the wild martagon lily to leave clean, spotless white, nodding, strongly reflexed Turk's-cap flowers with contrasting orange anthers, carried in tall racemes above whorled foliage. It typically grows taller and a touch more slender than the pink-purple species, and its pale flowers show up especially well against dark evergreen backdrops or in a partly shaded white-and-green border. Like the species, it resents transplanting and disturbance once settled, so choose a permanent shaded or partly shaded spot under high deciduous canopy and leave the clump undisturbed for years. Established plantings slowly bulk up and self-sow to form a long-lived colony requiring almost no maintenance beyond an annual mulch top-up.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Lilium martagon var. album

planting.note: Plant rhizomatous bulbs in fall or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; give this stout selection extra room, since it grows considerably taller and bulkier than the typical leopard lily.

directions: Giganteum is a robust, large-flowered form of the western native leopard lily, first found along the Van Duzen River in Northern California, that towers over the typical species at up to seven feet with whorls of leaves ascending thick stalks. Each stem can carry up to thirty reflexed, orange-and-crimson, red-spotted flowers stacked in tiers, a dramatically fuller display than the species produces, making it an imposing back-of-border presence along a partly shaded stream bank or woodland edge. It tolerates somewhat drier soil at root depth than the typical leopard lily while still preferring consistent moisture, and it is more heat-tolerant than most western native lilies. Leave the foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom to recharge the rhizomatous bulbs for the following season.
sources: Calscape (California Native Plant Society) — Lilium pardalinum 'Giganteum'

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall four to six inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the wild species sends up several orange-scarlet flowers per stem and naturalizes more reliably than large hybrid tulips.

directions: Tulipa praestans is a wild species tulip from the mountains of Tajikistan, distinguished from most garden tulips by its habit of opening three to five brilliant orange-scarlet, cup-shaped flowers from a single stem rather than the solitary bloom typical of hybrids. The gray-green leaves are downy and fringed with fine hairs along the margin, giving the foliage a slightly fuzzy texture that sets it apart at a glance from smoother-leaved tulips. Selections such as 'Fusilier' and 'Shogun' have been bred from this species, but the wild form itself remains a vigorous, reliable naturalizer in lean, sharply drained soil. Plant it in a rock garden, gravel bed, or front-of-border drift where its multi-flowered clusters can be appreciated up close, and allow the foliage to yellow fully after bloom before removing it.

common_name: Jenningsii Dwarf Taro (Silver-Blotched Black Velvet Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Divide corms or separate offsets in spring, or plant container-grown starts in moist, humus-rich soil in light to partial shade after frost; Jenningsii stays smaller than the species and suits pots, pond margins, and small shaded beds.

directions: Jenningsii is the most striking named selection of dwarf velvet taro, its small, glossy, arrow-shaped leaves a deep charcoal-black overlaid with dark central veins and a distinctive silvery-gray blotch radiating out from the leaf base, a pattern sharper and more jewel-like than the plainer dark veining of unselected seedlings. It stays lower and more compact than the species, forming a tidy clump well suited to shaded container groupings or the edge of a pond or bog garden where its dark color reads clearly against lighter companions. Keep the soil consistently moist to wet, since this taro relative naturally grows in wet, shaded ground, and provide light dappled shade rather than the deeper shade some Colocasia tolerate, since a bit of brightness helps sustain the silver blotch. Where winters drop much below 20°F, lift and store the corms indoors, or grow it as a striking warm-season container accent.
